uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether the child is notified or whether the child is of an age where separate awareness controls apply.

title: Data subject may lack control over who can view the child's location
description: If the backend allows the parent alone to invite additional guardians, the child may have limited or no ability to set preferences regarding which parties can access their location data. This creates a lack-of-control risk over disclosure preferences.
assumptions: Assumes the child has privacy interests in the location data and the system does not provide meaningful preference controls for the child or other relevant data subjects.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the child's age, legal role of the parent, and whether any preference or consent controls exist.

title: Invitation-based sharing may rely on invalid or insufficient consent/lawful basis
description: Sharing a child's location with an additional guardian is a new disclosure context involving sensitive personal data about a child. If the backend enables this sharing without a valid lawful basis, appropriate authorization, or required consent arrangements, the processing may be unlawful.
assumptions: Assumes the jurisdiction or policy requires a valid lawful basis and possibly consent/authorization for extending access to child location data.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction, parental authority model, and service terms; the flow alone does not confirm invalid consent.

title: Invitation metadata can create attributable evidence of the parent's sharing action
description: Backend handling of the invitation will typically generate metadata such as sender account, recipient identifier, timestamp, child account reference, and invitation status. This metadata can later be used to attribute the sharing action to the parent, reducing deniability.
assumptions: Assumes normal backend logging or invitation recordkeeping.

title: Backend responses may reveal whether the invited guardian exists or is reachable
description: When processing an invitation, system responses may differ depending on whether the supplied email, phone number, or account corresponds to an existing user or valid recipient. Such responses can reveal the existence of the invited person in the system or the validity of their contact details.
assumptions: Assumes the backend provides distinguishable responses for existing vs non-existing accounts or invitation states.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not specify response behavior, so this depends on implementation details.

title: Secondary guardian can link child location data with guardian-child relationship data
description: By granting access and sharing the child's live location with the secondary guardian, the backend enables combination of location data with relationship/context data about the child and guardians. This can make the child's movements linkable across sessions or contexts.
assumptions: Assumes the shared live location is associated with a specific child account or guardian relationship rather than being fully anonymous.

title: Live location sharing includes revealing attributes that can identify the child
description: A child's live location, especially when shared with account context granting access to a named secondary guardian, can reveal home, school, routines, or other attributes that support identification of the child even if direct identifiers are minimized.
assumptions: Assumes the secondary guardian receives location in a context tied to a specific child profile or household.

title: Location-sharing records may create attributable evidence about the child and guardians
description: Backend records or transmitted data showing that access was granted and live location was shared can later be used as evidence that a particular child was at a certain place and that a guardian relationship or sharing action existed, reducing deniability.
assumptions: Assumes the system logs or stores the grant/share event or the transmitted location data.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly mention logging, so applicability depends on whether the backend retains records or metadata of the sharing event.

title: Granting access reveals the existence of a child and active location-sharing relationship
description: The backend response and resulting access for the secondary guardian can reveal that a specific child exists in the system and that live location sharing is active for that child. This enables detection of the child's presence or enrollment in the service.
assumptions: Assumes the secondary guardian can infer from successful access grant that the child is registered and currently shareable/tracked.

title: Sharing live location may disclose more granular location data than necessary
description: Providing live location to the secondary guardian may expose precise, continuous whereabouts rather than a less granular status or approximate area, disclosing more sensitive personal data than functionally necessary for access sharing.
assumptions: Assumes 'live location' means precise or near-real-time coordinates rather than coarse location.

title: Child may be unaware that live location is disclosed to a secondary guardian
description: The backend grants a secondary guardian access and shares the child's live location, but the child as data subject may not be aware that this disclosure occurs, to whom it occurs, or under what conditions.
assumptions: Assumes the child is the data subject and is not automatically notified or informed about this sharing.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether the child is informed, so this depends on product transparency mechanisms.

title: Sharing live location with a secondary guardian may rely on invalid or insufficient consent
description: Granting a secondary guardian access to a child's live location may be unlawful if valid consent or another appropriate lawful basis for this disclosure is absent, unclear, or not properly managed.
assumptions: Assumes this processing is subject to consent or another lawful-basis requirement for child location sharing.
uncertainty_note: The applicable lawful basis is not provided, so this is a plausible compliance threat rather than a confirmed violation.

title: Aggregated analytics may enable group-level profiling by the partner
description: Even if the backend shares aggregated usage and engagement analytics rather than raw user records, the receiving advertising/analytics partner can use those aggregates to profile cohorts or groups of users and link observations across campaigns, app versions, regions, or time periods. This creates a linking risk at the source because the backend discloses analytics in a form that may still support association of behavior patterns with groups.
assumptions: Assumes the shared aggregates are segmented by dimensions such as geography, device type, campaign, time window, or feature usage, making repeated observations linkable across disclosures.
uncertainty_note: The flow description says 'aggregated' analytics, which reduces direct individual linking risk; this threat is included because sufficiently granular aggregates can still support group-level linking.

title: Partner may link received aggregates with its existing datasets for broader group profiling
description: The advertising/analytics partner may combine the received aggregated analytics with its own cross-client or market datasets to link app audience segments to broader behavioral or commercial profiles. This creates a linking threat at the destination because the partner is positioned to associate the disclosed analytics with other knowledge it already holds.
assumptions: Assumes the partner operates across multiple clients or campaigns and maintains additional datasets that can be correlated with the received analytics.
uncertainty_note: No explicit statement confirms dataset combination by the partner, but such combination is a common capability of advertising/analytics partners.

title: Small or highly segmented aggregates may allow singling out of individuals
description: If the backend shares aggregated analytics over very small cohorts, rare behaviors, or narrow time windows, the anonymity set may become too small and an individual user could become distinguishable despite the data being labeled aggregated. This is an identifying threat at the source because the backend determines the granularity of the shared analytics.
assumptions: Assumes some reports may concern low-volume segments, niche features, sparse geographies, or short reporting intervals.
uncertainty_note: The description does not specify aggregation thresholds or k-anonymity-style controls, so identifiability depends on implementation details not provided.

title: Partner may derive identifiable insights from aggregated analytics when combined with external knowledge
description: At the destination, the partner may use revealing attributes in the received analytics, such as region, device class, campaign, time period, or engagement pattern, together with external information to infer the identity of a person or a very small set of persons behind a segment.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include multiple dimensions or contextual attributes and the partner has auxiliary information.
uncertainty_note: Because only 'aggregated usage and engagement analytics' are described, this is a conditional risk rather than a certain one.

title: Shared engagement analytics can reveal existence and activity of user segments
description: By sending usage and engagement analytics to the partner, the backend may reveal whether particular user segments, features, campaigns, or behaviors exist and are active in the app. This is a detecting threat because the analytics themselves act as side effects that expose the presence or intensity of user activity.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics are broken down by meaningful segments or events rather than only a single global total.
uncertainty_note: Detection here is primarily at segment or cohort level; the flow description does not support strong claims about detecting specific individuals.

title: Propagation of analytics to an external partner may exceed what is necessary for app functionality
description: The backend propagates usage and engagement analytics to an external advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier. While commercially useful, this disclosure is not strictly necessary to deliver the app's core functionality to users, creating a data disclosure threat through propagation to another service.
assumptions: Assumes 'fund the app's free tier' is a business objective rather than a technical necessity for providing the app feature requested by the user.

title: Personal data exposure to a predetermined external party
description: The backend makes analytics accessible to a known external advertising/analytics partner. Even if the recipient set is fixed and anticipated, sharing user-related analytics with an outside party increases exposure beyond the app operator and creates a disclosure threat.
assumptions: Assumes the aggregated analytics still qualify as personal data or personal-data-derived information in context, especially if segmentable or re-linkable.
uncertainty_note: If the analytics are truly anonymized and non-personal, this threat would be weaker; the description does not establish that level of anonymization.

title: Users may be unaware that their usage data contributes to partner-facing analytics
description: Users of the app may not realize that their usage and engagement data is aggregated and shared with an advertising/analytics partner to monetize the free tier. This creates unawareness of processing at the source.
assumptions: Assumes this sharing is not made prominently visible in the user experience or privacy notice.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether notice is provided, so this is a plausible but unconfirmed threat.

title: Users may lack meaningful preference or consent controls over analytics sharing
description: If the backend shares aggregated usage analytics with the partner without offering users a clear opt-in, opt-out, or granular preference mechanism, data subjects may lack control over this secondary processing for advertising/analytics purposes.
assumptions: Assumes no effective in-app control exists for this sharing.
uncertainty_note: No consent or preference mechanism is described, so the threat is inferred from the absence of stated controls rather than explicit evidence.

title: Potential violation of data minimization in partner analytics sharing
description: Sharing usage and engagement analytics with an external advertising/analytics partner to support monetization may involve processing more personal-data-derived information, or exposing it to more parties, than is necessary for the app's primary service. This creates a non-compliance risk under data minimization principles.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics are personal data or remain attributable/relatable to users or user segments in context.
uncertainty_note: Whether data minimization is violated depends on the exact necessity assessment, aggregation level, and applicable legal interpretation.

title: Potential invalid consent or insufficient lawful basis for analytics sharing with partner
description: If the backend relies on consent for sharing analytics with an advertising/analytics partner, that consent may be invalid if it is not specific, informed, freely given, and revocable. If consent is not used, the chosen lawful basis may still be challenged given the monetization purpose and third-party disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes applicable law requires a lawful basis for this disclosure and that the analytics are not fully anonymized.
uncertainty_note: The flow description provides no information about lawful basis, consent design, or jurisdiction, so this is a plausible compliance threat rather than a confirmed defect.

title: Potential lack of support for data subject control over shared analytics
description: If users cannot access, object to, erase, or otherwise influence how their usage data is included in analytics shared with the partner, the system may fail to support relevant data subject rights and controls.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics remain within scope of applicable privacy rights and that no effective rights-handling process exists for this downstream sharing.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not mention rights mechanisms, so this is inferred from missing context.

title: Check-in message and location can be linked to the same child over time
description: The child-originated SOS/check-in flow likely contains a stable account, device, or child reference together with location and message content, enabling repeated events to be linked to the same child across time.
uncertainty_note: The exact identifier is not shown in the flow description, but some stable reference is typically required so the backend can associate the message with the correct child/parent relationship.

title: Location-bearing SOS message makes the child identifiable
description: Current location combined with the fact that the sender is a child in a parent-child safety context can reveal or strongly support identification of the child, even if direct real-name fields are not present in the payload.
uncertainty_note: This may also involve direct identifiers in practice, but the description only explicitly states message plus current location.

title: SOS/check-in record can be used as attributable evidence of the child's action
description: A manual check-in or SOS submission creates a record that can later be attributed to the child, reducing plausible deniability about having sent the alert or being at the reported location at that time.

title: Transmission of an SOS/check-in can reveal that the child is active or in a noteworthy situation
description: Observation of this communication can reveal that the child has initiated a manual check-in or SOS event, which may disclose presence, activity, or a potentially urgent situation even before reading full content.
uncertainty_note: This depends on whether an observer can distinguish this flow from ordinary app traffic.

title: Backend may receive more precise location granularity than necessary for parent notification
description: The flow sends the child's current location to the backend; if exact coordinates are transmitted when a coarser area would suffice for the intended parent alerting function, the backend receives more fine-grained personal data than necessary.
uncertainty_note: Whether exact precision is necessary depends on product requirements for SOS handling, which are not fully specified.

title: Child may lack control over what location data is shared during manual check-in/SOS
description: If the app/backend does not let the child choose whether to include location, adjust precision, or understand the consequences of sending an SOS/check-in, the child has limited control over processing of their personal data in this flow.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether controls or preferences exist; threat included because this flow inherently involves sensitive child location sharing.

title: Processing exact child location in SOS/check-in may violate data minimization if not strictly needed
description: Because this flow involves sensitive child location data, collecting and processing precise current location for each manual check-in/SOS could exceed what is necessary for the stated purpose unless precision and scope are demonstrably justified.
uncertainty_note: Assessment of actual non-compliance depends on the lawful purpose and whether precise location is necessary for the service design.
